What these diagrams show

Short answer

Fourteen flows cover every use case of one app's Kaneki Auth deployment: seven account flows, four OAuth flows for external apps, and three machine/admin flows. Each is drawn from the Better Auth 1.7.19 source, so the endpoints and database writes match what the library actually does. S1S2

How to read the diagrams

Arrows

  • Solid dark: a request
  • Dashed grey: a response or redirect
  • Solid green: a database read/write on the app's Neon project
  • Solid orange: mail sent through sendMail() (Gmail SMTP in phase 1)
  • Loop: work done inside one participant
  • Yellow bar: transaction boundary, branch, or user action

Participants

  • Kaneki Auth: one app's deployment, <app>-auth.vercel.app, all routes under /api/auth
  • Neon: that app's own database (separate per app)
  • Client app / App backend / Resource API: the external app's parts
  • Steps are numbered per diagram

Route paths are the endpoint paths in the code with the default /api/auth base path. Shorter labels such as /oauth2/token mean the same prefix. S2

Signing up and signing in

The three sign-in methods chosen for the service, plus password sign-up. All of them end the same way: a session row and a session cookie on the auth deployment's domain. S5

Sign up with email + password

UC-01 One request creates the user, the password account and (by default) a session inside a single transaction, then emails a verification link.

  • If the email already exists and email verification is required, the endpoint returns a generic response so it does not reveal which emails are registered. S1
  • The verification link carries a signed JWT, not a database row. It expires after 3600 s by default. S6
  • Mail goes through the sendMail() interface (Gmail SMTP in phase 1), so the send must be awaited. S4S7

Sign in with email + password

UC-03 Look up the user, compare the password hash, create a session.

  • An unknown email still runs a dummy hash so response time does not reveal whether the account exists. S8 INFERRED (purpose read from the code, not documented)
  • Placing the rate-limit check before the handler is a simplification of the middleware order. INFERRED

Sign in with Google

UC-04 A standard OAuth round trip to Google. On return, Better Auth either creates a user, links Google to an existing same-email user, or refreshes the stored Google tokens.

  • The Google redirect URI for each app deployment is https://<app>-auth.vercel.app/api/auth/callback/google, and baseURL must be set. S12
  • Because each app has its own database, the same Google account creates separate users in app 1 and app 2. S4

Sign in with a magic link

UC-05 Two requests: one stores a short-lived token and mails the link, the other consumes the token and signs the user in, creating them if needed.

  • Set disableSignUp: true on apps that should be invite-only. S14
  • Default plugin rate limit: 5 requests per 60 s. S14

Verification, reset and sign-out

Verify email

UC-02 Clicking the link checks the JWT signature and flips emailVerified. No verification row is read.

  • The same endpoint also handles change-of-email confirmations (the token carries updateTo). S6

Reset a forgotten password

UC-06 Store a reset token, mail it, then swap it for a new password inside one transaction.

  • Unknown emails trigger a dummy verification lookup, so timing does not reveal account existence. S15 INFERRED (purpose read from the code)
  • revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset signs the user out everywhere. Recommended on. S15

Sign out

UC-07 Delete the session row and clear the cookie.

    External apps (OAuth / OIDC)

    These flows are how a separate app on another domain uses Kaneki Auth. They rely on the account flows above for the actual sign-in. S17

    External app: authorize, consent, code exchange

    UC-09 · UC-10 The core OIDC flow. The browser carries the user to Kaneki Auth and back. The app then swaps the code for tokens server-side.

    • The resource must exist in oauthResource, or the request fails with invalid_target. If per-client resources are enforced, the client must also be linked through oauthClientResource. S2
    • Without resource the access token is opaque and is stored in oauthAccessToken instead of being signed. S18S2
    • Reusing a code fails at step 12 and also revokes the tokens issued from that code. S2

    External app calls its API

    UC-14 · UC-15 With a JWT, the API checks the token locally against cached public keys. Only the opaque-token fallback calls back to Kaneki Auth.

      Refresh tokens (rotation)

      UC-11 Each refresh token works once. Using it returns a new access token and a new refresh token, and retires the old one.

      • The rotationReplayResponse and rotationReplayExpiresAt columns suggest a short grace window for a retried refresh. S21 INFERRED (behaviour not traced)

      External app logs the user out

      UC-13 The app revokes its refresh token, then sends the browser to the end-session endpoint so the Kaneki Auth session ends too.

      • The database operations in steps 2 and 5 are not traced line by line. INFERRED
      • End-session works only for clients with enableEndSession and registered postLogoutRedirectUris. S21 INFERRED

      Machines and admins

      Machine-to-machine: client credentials

      UC-16 A backend gets a 1-hour JWT for itself (no user) and calls the API, which verifies it offline.

      • The grant is off for every client until an admin allows it. openid, profile, email and offline_access cannot be requested. S18

      API keys: create and use

      UC-17 · UC-22 Keys are created through the API and shown once. In 1.7.19 they can only be verified inside the auth server, so they suit calls to Kaneki Auth's own routes.

      • Correction to the architecture doc: there is no public POST /api-key/verify in 1.7.19. verifyApiKey is created with createAuthEndpoint.serverOnly. To accept API keys you add your own route in the auth deployment that calls it. S3

      Admin registers a client app and its API

      UC-18 · UC-19 Before an app can use SD-08, an admin creates its OAuth client and the resource (API) its tokens are for.

      • How the admin check works for these routes (step 2), and whether the secret is stored hashed, was not traced. INFERRED

      Open questions found while drawing

      1. Admin bootstrap: how is the first admin created in each app's database (seed script, or a config list of admin user ids)? OPEN
      2. API key route: do you need API keys at all in phase 1? If yes, which custom route(s) should accept them (SD-13)? OPEN
      3. Per-client resources: turn on enforcePerClientResources, so each client can only get tokens for APIs it is linked to? Recommended. S2 OPEN
      4. Auto sign-in after sign-up while email is unverified: allow it, or set requireEmailVerification? OPEN
